why: The first use of the BST ordering to steer a search: a node below low can only have useful values in its right subtree, one above high only in its left, so whole subtrees are skipped.
hints: If node.val < low, can anything in its left subtree be in range?
Below low: go right only. Above high: go left only. In range: add the value and visit both children.
DFS with a stack; the work is proportional to the nodes in range plus the two boundary paths, O(n) in the worst case.
pitfalls: Do not stop at an out-of-range node: its other subtree can still hold values in range.
The range is inclusive at both ends.
